case_study_insert.main_stem: Sentinel Flow Systems (SFS) is a public limited company in the plastics manufacturing sector, producing high-density polyethylene pipe and fittings for water utilities and drainage contractors, with a workforce of 95. Founded in 1997 by Helena Voss and led by chief executive Marcus Bell since 2015, SFS operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. SFS plans to invest $1,450,000 in a twin-screw extrusion line for large-diameter pipe, financed by a $900,000 new share issue and $550,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $405,000 a year, a variable cost of $19.00 a unit and a selling price of $28.00, and produces 90,000 units a year. SFS faces a skills gap in CNC programming and labour turnover of 19%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The extrusion line produced 22,500 pipe lengths last quarter at a defect rate of 1.9%, down from 3.6% a year ago; regrind waste fell from 7.2% to 4.8% of resin throughput. Customer complaints fell from 31 to 17 per month. Average extrusion set-up time improved to 1.6 hours. A survey of 260 utility specifiers found that 54% would adopt larger-diameter pipe for new mains contracts and 41% prioritise lead-free certification. 22 of 95 staff need CNC programming upskilling; the off-the-job automation course costs $1,050 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Sentinel Flow Systems as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.10% to 5.90%, the sixth rise this year. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $13.70 to $14.67 per hour from April 2026, squeezing manufacturers' labour costs. (3) HDPE resin input costs have risen 14.6% year-on-year and input-cost inflation in plastics is running at 7.8%, while water-utility capital expenditure grew 4.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: SFS plans to finance part of its large-diameter pipe line with a $900,000 new share issue. Explain two advantages for SFS of using retained profit instead of the share issue.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit is free of issue costs and carries no expectation of dividends, so SFS keeps more cash to fund the $1,450,000 twin-screw extrusion line without diluting ordinary shareholders. Existing shareholders would see their stake diluted if the new issue is large, whereas retained profit rewards them directly through the capital growth the new line will generate.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids signalling. Announcing a big share issue can be read by the market as SFS struggling to fund itself internally, knocking the share price and raising the cost of future capital before the pipe line proves itself. Using the $550,000 retained profit — built from years of supplying water utilities — demonstrates that SFS self-funds expansions, protects Helena Voss's and Marcus Bell's credibility with institutional holders, and keeps control squarely with current owners rather than new subscribers who might demand board influence or strategy changes.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Sentinel Flow Systems and its extrusion-line expansion.

questions.question_text: SFS is launching its large-diameter pipe to water utilities. Consider exhibiting at the International Water Infrastructure Exhibition, advertising in the Utilities Weekly trade press, or a targeted LinkedIn campaign aimed at procurement engineers. Which should SFS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
International Water Infrastructure Exhibition: A stand at the industry's flagship expo, absorbing a sizeable slice of the $1,450,000 line's budget, puts SFS in front of the exact 54% of utility specifiers who told its survey they would adopt larger-diameter pipe for new mains. Live flow and pressure demonstrations and EN-certified samples are persuasive for capital purchases, and one framework agreement with a regional utility could book out the twin-screw line's first-year capacity. Cost and staff-time are the drawbacks, plus a long tail of low-quality leads.

Utilities Weekly trade press: Quarter-page adverts costing only a few thousand dollars an issue reach engineers and procurement officers nationwide between buying cycles, reinforce the 41% lead-free-certification message with technical detail, and cost far less than an expo stand. However, print readership is shrinking, response is hard to attribute, and a single ad will not close a multi-year mains framework contract.

Targeted LinkedIn campaign for procurement engineers: Promoted content segmented by job title (procurement, network engineering, asset management) costs a modest five-figure sum each quarter, delivers measurable click-throughs to SFS's technical datasheet pack, and keeps SFS visible through long tender cycles. Engagement is opt-in and measurable, but conversion to signed frameworks is slow and depends on follow-up by the technical sales team.

Recommendation: SFS should choose the International Water Infrastructure Exhibition. Capital purchases of mains pipe are relationship and specification decisions made face-to-face between utility engineers and credible manufacturers; the expo is the only channel where all target specifiers converge in one place. Utilities Weekly is rejected as too passive and hard to measure for a launch; LinkedIn is rejected as an inadequate sole channel for a considered, committee-approved mains contract, though it is the ideal low-cost nurture channel between exhibitions and tender deadlines.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SFS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SFS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade press and LinkedIn are rejected as the lead channel.

questions.question_text: SFS uses a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for SFS of democratic leadership for its 95 employees.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership inside SFS's hierarchy keeps the 95 machine operators, maintenance techs and finishers engaged despite clear layers of authority from chief executive Marcus Bell down to cell supervisors. Operators involved in setting extrusion speeds and regrind-handling routines commit to quality outcomes, helping push the defect rate from 3.6% to 1.9% and regrind waste from 7.2% to 4.8% without heavy-handed supervision.

Point 2: Consultation surfaces practical problems that supervisors cannot see from the control room — for example the CNC-programming bottleneck now affecting 22 staff, and the causes of the 19% labour turnover among younger operators. Fixing these with the workforce rather than around it improves retention, protects the 90,000-unit output programme for the water utilities, and strengthens the internal promotion pipeline that SFS needs as it prepares the large-diameter line for exactly the 54% of specifiers ready to adopt it. Open consultation on shift patterns also gives SFS early visibility of seasonal peaks in mains-laying demand, so supervisors can roster the 95 staff against the 90,000-unit programme rather than scrambling for overtime once orders land.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SFS's defects, skills gap and turnover.

questions.question_text: SFS must end the manual bottleneck at the finishing bays. Consider replacing the manual end-facing and drilling stations with three automated CAM cells, or retaining the finishing crews and upskilling them in CNC programming. Which should SFS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Three automated CAM cells: Automating end-facing and drilling would raise throughput, eliminate the dimensional variability that aged into the 1.9% defect rate and free skilled staff for inspection and set-up. Defects would fall further, complaint counts below 17 per month would drop, and lead times for mains contracts would shorten — a decisive edge when utilities run penalty clauses. Drawbacks are a capital price far beyond the training budget, displacement of long-serving finishers in a PLC with shareholder scrutiny of social impact, and heavier dependence on specialist CNC programmers SFS does not yet have.

Retaining crews with CNC upskilling: The off-the-job automation course at $1,050 per employee for the 22 staff who need programming costs $23,100 — a fraction of CAM cells — and builds loyalty exactly where 19% labour turnover is bleeding experienced hands. It aligns with democratic consultation (crews help select the syllabus), keeps valuable flexibility for short runs of small custom fittings, and preserves social licence with the workforce and local community. Drawbacks are slower output growth, continued exposure to human error, and a risk that upskilled staff immediately resign for higher CAM-lab salaries elsewhere.

Decision: SFS should retain the finishing crews and fund the CNC upskilling now, while piloting one automated CAM cell alongside the extrusion line. This sequence attacks the skills gap at its root for $23,100, halves defect risk on the sensitive end-facing operation, and honours the democratic compact with employees before automation is layered in. Installing three CAM cells immediately is rejected because the 22-person programming gap would leave the machines underrun, morale would collapse under visible redundancy risk, and the $1,450,000 share-issue-funded extrusion line already stretches capital commitments. One pilot cell is the measured middle step SFS needs before scaling automation fully.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the automation and training options with limited application to SFS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of CAM automation versus crew upskilling in the context of SFS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of SFS with a well-justified decision covering capital cost, skills, morale and risk.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SFS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $405,000 ÷ ($28.00 − $19.00) = $405,000 ÷ $9.00 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $28.00 − $19.00 = $9.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $9.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SFS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 45,000-unit break-even output with current production of 90,000 units to confirm the pipe line is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 45,000 units — a hundred percent headroom — before approving the full large-diameter ramp-up.
2. A contribution per unit of $9.00 lets SFS model tenders for water-utility mains contracts, for example a 5% volume discount to $26.60 would cut contribution to $7.60, showing bidders exactly how many extra lengths make a low-price bid accretive rather than dilutive.
3. Fixed costs of $405,000 combined with the $9.00 contribution tests whether the $1,450,000 twin-screw line, funded by a $900,000 share issue and $550,000 retained profit, can generate the operating surplus needed to fund phase-two automation without another share issue.
4. Unit cost data ($405,000 ÷ 90,000 units + $19.00 = $23.50) lets managers benchmark quarterly progress, target the regrind waste (down from 7.2% to 4.8%) for further reduction, renegotiate HDPE resin contracts amid 14.6% input inflation, and set labour productivity targets of about 947 units per worker (90,000 ÷ 95) to plan crews around the 19% labour turnover.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units ($405,000 ÷ $9.00) | (ii) Contribution per unit = $9.00 ($28.00 − $19.00) | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 45,000 units (100% headroom) against 90,000-unit output; utility-tender discount modelling (5% off = $26.60, contribution $7.60) against $405,000 fixed costs; feasibility check for the $1,450,000 twin-screw extrusion line funded by a $900,000 share issue and $550,000 retained profit; unit-cost benchmarking at $23.50 against the 4.8% regrind waste, 14.6% HDPE resin inflation and about 947 units per worker productivity.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SFS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SFS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.80 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.87 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.05 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $380,000 inventories + $250,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $720,000; 2025 current assets = $310,000 + $265,000 + $135,000 = $710,000. 2024: $720,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.80; 2025: $710,000 ÷ $380,000 = 1.87. For the stricter measure, 2024: ($720,000 − $380,000) ÷ $400,000 = $340,000 ÷ $400,000 = 0.85; 2025: ($710,000 − $310,000) ÷ $380,000 = $400,000 ÷ $380,000 = 1.05.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved, and the improvement is high quality. Inventories fell from $380,000 to $310,000 as the extrusion line's set-up time came down to 1.6 hours and regrind waste fell to 4.8%, releasing cash into the business; at the same time cash rose from $90,000 to $135,000 and current liabilities fell from $400,000 to $380,000. The acid test moved through the critical 1.00 threshold to 1.05, so SFS can now cover short-term debts without selling pipe inventory — real headroom while digesting a $1,450,000 capital programme funded largely by a share issue. One caution: trade receivables rose from $250,000 to $265,000, and water-utility payment cycles are typically 45-60 days; if mains contracts bunch at quarter-end, cash could tighten again before the large-diameter line reaches full output.

Conclusion: SFS's financial position has improved. Liquidity strengthened on both measures with lower inventories, lower liabilities and a cash balance up 50%, and the improvement is not inventory-led. SFS should continue tightening utility credit terms, protect the $135,000 cash buffer, and avoid further near-term debt-funded capex until the twin-screw line demonstrates stable margins on the 54% of specifiers already committed to large-diameter mains.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether SFS's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SFS of introducing a formal quality assurance programme rather than relying on final quality control inspection alone.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Quality assurance builds prevention into every extrusion batch — resin testing, in-line diameter gauging, operator checkpoints and documented set-up verification — rather than catching defects at final inspection. For SFS this compounds the gains already visible in the 1.9% defect rate (down from 3.6%) and the 4.8% regrind waste, meaning fewer rejected pipe lengths shipped to water utilities, fewer site failures under warranty, and a stronger bid position where 41% of specifiers demand lead-free certification evidenced by audited process records.

Disadvantage: Prevention costs money and discipline up front: calibrated gauges, documented procedures, and extra operator time on the twin-screw line could add tens of thousands of dollars a year, plus training for the 22 staff already behind on CNC programming. QA also requires every worker to follow the system religiously; one bypassed checkpoint silently invalidates the whole audit trail, and in SFS's hierarchical structure, supervisors may rubber-stamp the forms without genuinely checking — turning an assurance programme into paperwork theatre that fails the first utility audit.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SFS's defect rate, certification and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.90%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 14.6% rise in HDPE resin input costs will affect SFS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise to 5.90%: SFS carries no bank debt at the moment — its $1,450,000 programme is funded by a $900,000 share issue and $550,000 retained profit — so the direct cost of the 0.80% rise is limited to short-term working-capital facilities, which will be minimal. The indirect effects matter more: utility customers' own capital budgets may slow, and SFS's cost of equity could drift if income yields look less attractive against deposits at 5.9%.

Minimum wage increase of 7.1% to $14.67: SFS's 95 staff span operators, maintenance, finishing and packing. If average earnings sit near $14.67 an hour for 2,080 hours, each worker adds about $2,023 a year, or roughly $192,000 across the workforce — a heavy, unavoidable hit against $405,000 of fixed costs, only partly offset by the productivity gains of the new twin-screw line (about 947 units per worker) and by natural wastage control.

HDPE resin input cost inflation of 14.6%: Resin is the dominant element of SFS's $19.00 variable cost, roughly $10.50-$11.50 per unit. A 14.6% rise adds about $1.53-$1.68 per unit; across 90,000 units that is roughly $138,000-$151,000 a year, compressing contribution per unit from $9.00 toward $7.30-$7.45, eroding the return behind the $1,450,000 expansion and squeezing margin of safety.

Conclusion: The 7.1% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. At roughly $192,000 a year it exceeds the resin impact (~$138,000-$151,000) and vastly outweighs the interest-rate effect (minimal), and labour cost cannot be substituted away quickly — automation takes quarters to implement. With fixed mains-contract pricing, SFS should accelerate the CAM-cell pilot, renegotiate utility framework prices on the 4.8% growth in utility capex, and freeze discretionary spend until the wage rise annualises in payroll.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SFS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SFS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SFS with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
